#6006. The Most Frequent JetBlue Airbus A320 Routes In 2026

JetBlue’s busiest Airbus A320 route in 2026 is not a transcontinental link between two major business centers. According to Cirium, it is Orlando–San Juan, a leisure-heavy connection that recorded 3,562 flights in both directions in the supplied flight-tracking dataset. More revealing still, all 11 busiest A320 city pairs touch Florida, putting the airline’s New York roots alongside a network heavily concentrated in the Sunshine State.

That pattern raises a question a route ranking alone cannot answer: is JetBlue deliberately building a deeper Florida operation, or taking advantage of a gap left by the defunct Spirit Airlines while trying to improve its financial performance? The answer involves Orlando’s reach, Fort Lauderdale’s rapid expansion, the difference between counting flights and measuring capacity, and the A320’s role as JetBlue reshapes its fleet.

Orlando–San Juan sits at the center of the pattern because it combines frequency with meaningful distance. JetBlue operated 1,782 flights from Orlando International Airport (MCO) to Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), offering 286,596 seats, and another 1,780 in the opposite direction, offering 286,380. Together, that is 3,562 flights and 572,976 seats across an average sector length of 1,189 miles (1,914 km).

The route generated approximately 681.3 million available seat miles (ASMs), or around 1.1 billion available seat kilometers. ASMs multiply the seats offered by the distance flown; they measure capacity, not passengers carried. The near-identical totals in each direction also suggest demand is relatively balanced rather than dominated by one-way seasonal traffic.

The route links two of the five cities where JetBlue described itself as a leading carrier in its January 2026 announcement: Orlando and San Juan. Leisure travelers and people visiting friends and relatives give the route more than one source of demand, helping support frequency without relying on traditional corporate traffic. But the lead over Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia is only 212 flights, or about 6%. Why, then, is Fort Lauderdale becoming such a consequential part of the airline’s plans?

Fort Lauderdale’s importance is rooted in JetBlue’s history as well as its current expansion. The airline’s first revenue flight in February 2000 connected New York-JFK with Fort Lauderdale. More than 25 years later, Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia remains one of its busiest A320 corridors, with 3,350 combined flights and 542,688 seats across 1,076 miles (1,732 km). Fort Lauderdale–San Juan follows with 3,280 flights and 531,288 seats over 1,046 miles (1,683 km).

The immediate catalyst is Spirit Airlines’ collapse. JetBlue moved to fill part of the gap and said it intended to reach around 150 daily departures from Fort Lauderdale by year-end. Its July announcement put summer departures near 130, more than 75% above 2025 levels, while adding service to destinations including Baltimore, Charlotte, Cleveland, Nashville, Detroit, Houston, Chicago and Ponce. CBS Miami reported on the expansion as an effort to fill gaps left by Spirit.

The plan is about more than replacing individual routes. As documented by Aviation Week, JetBlue has discussed as many as 370 connecting itineraries through Fort Lauderdale, giving the airport a larger role in the network. The fixed flight dataset may under-represent recently launched services, so the current route mix is a snapshot rather than a final picture of the expansion. The leading routes nevertheless show how Florida connects to JetBlue’s wider network:

JetBlue is doubling down at FLL just as Spirit Airlines is forced to pull back.

Orlando’s footprint is broader than the leading San Juan route suggests. Across the six city pairs in the 11-route group that cross Orlando, the airport accounts for 14,507 flights. Fort Lauderdale accounts for 10,981 across four pairs, while West Palm Beach contributes another 2,156 through its Westchester service. JetBlue’s Florida presence is therefore spread across three airports rather than resting on one dominant base.

Orlando represents about 52% of the flights in the 11-route group. Fort Lauderdale’s role is different: it combines New York services with Caribbean flying and a fast-growing list of new destinations. New York remains the other half of the pattern, with seven of the 11 city pairs connecting a New York-area airport — JFK, LaGuardia, Newark, or Westchester — with Florida. Boston and San Juan account for two pairs each.

The New York side is changing too. JFK’s New Terminal One has slipped to early 2027, while Terminal 6 is expected to host JetBlue, according to Simple Flying reporting. With service spread across four New York-area airports, the airline must balance geographic coverage against overlapping capacity. And flight totals alone cannot show which routes contribute most to the network’s capacity: how does the picture change when distance is included?

A flight count treats every departure equally, whether it covers 944 miles (1,519 km) or 1,237 miles (1,991 km). ASMs provide another perspective by multiplying seats offered by distance flown. Orlando–San Juan remains the largest route on this measure, at approximately 681.3 million ASMs. Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia follows with 583.9 million, while Fort Lauderdale–San Juan generates about 555.7 million.

The movement further down the network is more revealing. Fort Lauderdale–Boston recorded 2,151 flights over an average distance of 1,237 miles (1,991 km), producing about 430.7 million ASMs. Orlando–Boston operated more flights, at 2,222, but its shorter 1,121-mile (1,804-km) sector generated approximately 398.9 million ASMs. Fort Lauderdale–Boston therefore contributes more capacity despite operating fewer flights.

JetBlue’s third-quarter 2026 results underline why capacity and profitability must be considered separately. The airline reported an 18.4% increase in revenue per available seat mile (RASM), while average fuel reached $3.91 per gallon, 57% higher year over year. Its third-quarter results release also said BlueFirst, its new domestic first-class product, would begin operating on Boston–Fort Lauderdale on December 8. That longer route gains importance when capacity is measured in seat-miles, and the premium product suggests JetBlue sees an opportunity to earn more from at least some of its Florida services. What does the A320 cabin itself reveal about how the airline matches capacity to demand?

Discover the airline that consistently delivers the widest standard economy seats today, offering passengers a genuinely roomy cabin experience.

JetBlue and Simple Flying show two A320 layouts: the Classic configuration with 150 seats and the Restyled version with 162. The supplied flight data offers an indirect way to estimate where each may be used more often, although it cannot identify individual aircraft. Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia, Fort Lauderdale–San Juan, Fort Lauderdale–Newark, and Westchester–West Palm Beach average close to 162 seats per departure, pointing toward the higher-capacity Restyled aircraft.

Orlando–LaGuardia is different, averaging 158.9 seats per flight. If the two published layouts are the only configurations in the dataset, that average would be consistent with roughly one in four departures using the 150-seat Classic. This remains an inference, not a confirmed aircraft assignment, because aircraft swaps and schedule changes can affect route averages.

The 12-seat difference still matters at scale. Across 3,562 Orlando–San Juan flights, operating the 162-seat aircraft instead of the 150-seat version on every departure would represent as many as 42,744 additional seats. JetBlue continues to market 32 inches (81 centimeters) of economy pitch, but additional seats only improve the economics if they can be sold at fares that cover fuel, labor, and other operating costs. With the A320 accounting for 129 of JetBlue’s 298 aircraft as of September 30, 2026, how might the arrival of more A220s change that equation?

Fort Lauderdale’s expansion is expected to take the airport beyond 150 daily departures this winter. According to Simple Flying, citing Cirium schedule data, Fort Lauderdale is now JetBlue's busiest airport by scheduled departures, ahead of JFK and Boston, with roughly 21,500 winter departures against nearly 13,700 a year earlier. JetBlue’s July announcement included new services to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia, Indianapolis and Columbus, alongside routes launched earlier in the year. A Mint-equipped San Diego service was scheduled for November 19, while Caracas remained without a confirmed start date in the supplied material. Not every new route will use an A320, however.

Mint class requires the A321, and more premium flying from Fort Lauderdale could direct some growth toward larger aircraft rather than simply adding A320 frequencies. Meanwhile, JetBlue’s fleet plan lists seven A220 deliveries in 2027, nine in 2028, 10 in 2029, and two in 2030. The smaller A220 gives the airline another capacity option for markets where demand may not justify an A320, potentially allowing it to reserve larger aircraft for stronger corridors.

The fleet transition is taking place while JetBlue is still working to improve its finances. The supplied analysis cites Air Data News for a third-quarter loss of $257 million and a fall in cash from $1.95 billion at the end of 2025 to $1.26 billion in September; JetBlue is targeting sustained profitability in 2027. Yet the airline also reported that Fort Lauderdale’s RASM increased nearly 15% in the third quarter despite capacity growth of more than 65%. The test is whether that revenue performance can hold as more flights enter the schedule.

If JetBlue keeps adding capacity to established Florida routes, the network may become even more concentrated around Orlando and Fort Lauderdale. If A220 deliveries allow it to open thinner markets while reserving A320s and A321s for stronger corridors, the pattern could diversify. The route data captures a moment of rapid change; the next fleet and schedule decisions will show whether Florida is becoming JetBlue’s lasting growth engine or simply its biggest opportunity in 2026.

#6005. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

If you're flying this holiday season, be sure to check your airline profile before you head to the airport.

Millions of frequent flyers are now eligible for one of the best time-savers around ... but only if they sign up ahead of time.

Over the last few months, the Transportation Security Administration rapidly expanded its new TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program to dozens of the nation’s largest airports. The new program allows travelers to quickly pass through TSA checkpoints without having to pull out their boarding pass or ID.

It's now available at more than 60 hubs nationwide, and it's a great way to speed up your trip through airport security during the year's busiest travel months.

The TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program uses facial comparison technology to help travelers breeze through the first stage of the TSA checkpoint in a matter of seconds.

Travelers passing through these lanes get their picture taken as they approach the TSA officer, and the TSA’s computers compare that image to a passport photo on file.

Typically, travelers using these fast lanes can then speed through without pulling out their wallet or boarding pass. The experience is often faster than using any other security lane, even Clear.

TPG’s Clint Henderson wrote about his experience using the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes, which are typically marked by blue-and-green signage at checkpoints.

Read more: 8 ways to get free or discounted TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear

If you’re a TSA PreCheck member or get your TSA PreCheck access through Global Entry, you’re eligible to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes — as long as you opt in.

To opt in, you’ll want to go to your airline frequent flyer profile, upload an image of your passport and consent to the facial identification program.

For instance, ahead of a recent United Airlines flight out of Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), I pulled up my United app. I clicked on "TSA PreCheck and travel documents."

Then, I selected “TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.”

The app prompted me to add a photo of my passport, just like you might before an international flight.

And then there were a couple of pages where I had to opt in and consent. Once you do this, you should be cleared to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes.

This spring, the TSA completed an aggressive rollout of the new technology to more than 60 airports nationwide.

Each of the five largest U.S. carriers now partners with the administration to allow passengers access to the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes at many of the nation's largest hubs, as well as at a bunch of medium and smaller airports.

Here’s the full rundown of airlines and airports where it’s available as of November 2026:

You’ll only be able to use the TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes if your airline partners with the service at that specific airport and if you opt into the service with that specific carrier.

Also, keep in mind that there are cases (as shown above) where one airline allows Touchless ID access, while another at the same airport does not. When that discrepancy happens, it's typically because the new TSA technology is only available in certain terminals.

Take my home airport, Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), for example. Alaska Airlines and Southwest don't offer the service here because the TSA's Touchless technology isn't available at the smaller terminal where those carriers operate. But the new fast lanes are open in Terminal 2 for passengers flying with American, Delta and United.

You should still bring your Real ID or an acceptable alternative, like a passport, to the airport even if you've opted into TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.

As I've seen numerous times at airports, technology can malfunction, or some other snafu can arise that prompts officers to ask you to present a valid ID.

#6003. How Many Miles Per Gallon Does A Boeing 747 Get?

Phillip B. Espinasse | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

With its four engines, the Boeing 747 uses vast quantities of fuel, burning through 3,800 gallons every hour. This high fuel burn amounts to 0.9 gallons used every second and 0.19 miles per gallon (mpg). In this article, we will detail the Boeing 747's mpg further, including the mpg per traveler, and how this compares to travel in a car and in modern airliners.

We will also delve into ongoing debates around sustainable aviation fuel to explore if aviation can be sustainable. After all, all airliners burn through staggering quantities of fuel.

According to the BBC's Future Planet, a cruising 747 burns through 0.9 gallons (four liters) of fuel each second. This is equivalent to 3,500 gallons (13,250 liters) of fuel every hour. If a 747 is cruising at its standard cruising speed of around 580 mph (933 km/h), it is covering a mile every 6.2 seconds.

Covering a mile requires 5.9 gallons of fuel. As a result, a cruising Boeing 747 can achieve just 0.18 miles per gallon. However, this is not the full picture, as a 747 carries far more people than most aircraft. For example, Qantas' 747-400s carried 364 passengers across three classes.

If we extrapolate this number of seats into the mpg that each passenger has, the data shows 65.5 mpg per passenger. According to calculatormpg.co.uk, the baseline for a good car mpg is 50. If a car is carrying two people, then the car is achieving 100 passenger miles per gallon.

This suggests that flying on a 747 still uses substantially more fuel than a car carrying multiple people, but less than a car carrying one person. The other difference to consider when comparing fuel consumption across modes of transport is that a 747 has to take off, which is not a concern for a car or train.

Takeoff is the most fuel-intensive part of any flight as the jet has to get up to speed while it is at its heaviest, and then climb to cruising altitude. The exact fuel consumption during takeoff depends hugely on how close the aircraft is to its maximum takeoff weight (almost a million pounds). However, the general quantity of fuel needed is approximately 5,000 gallons (19,000 liters).

This consumption of fuel equates to a fuel burn of approximately 154,000 lbs (70,000 kg) for a flight from London to New York. To sustain such a high consumption, a 747 can carry a vast amount of fuel. The debut 747 could carry 48,400 gallons (183,000 liters) of fuel. Later variants increased this capacity to 63,034 gallons (238,610 liters) for the 747-8.

This vast ocean of fuel is stored primarily in the aircraft's wings. A 747 has two main fuel tanks in each wing, with further reserve fuel tanks in the wings' outer sections and central wing tanks. It is common for airliners to store fuel in the wings to free up fuselage space for cargo storage.

The primary fuel tanks are usually filled first. Any further fuel needed for the flight is put into the central wing tank. Any final drops needed are pumped into the reserve tanks. Select 747 models can increase fuel capacity further by sealing off part of the horizontal stabilizer and using it as an additional auxiliary tank.

In recent years, the 747-400F's fuel storage has come under FAA scrutiny due to improperly applied cap seals on some aircraft. Should these seals fail during a lightning strike or short circuit, it could allow arcing within the fuel tanks and cause an explosion.

The FAA's attention came following several fuel tank explosions on commercial aircraft in the late 1990s. This led to a 2001 review titled ‘Transport Airplane Fuel Tank System Design Review, Flammability Reduction, and Maintenance and Inspection Requirements.’

The document led to a range of safety recommendations, including those relating to cap seals. In June 2022, the FAA responded to reports that cap seals were not being applied properly during production of the 747-400F. A design change omitted the application of the cap seals on eight fasteners, distributed equally across both wings.

At a surface level, the similar MPG per traveler between a 747 and a modern car would suggest a similar amount of environmental harm. Moreover, the US Energy Information Administration claims that jet fuel produces 21.1 lbs of CO2 per gallon, which is comparable to the 19.6 lbs of greenhouse gas produced from burning a gallon of gasoline.

However, focusing on CO2 alone hides the unique environmental harm caused by burning aviation fuel at altitude. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change points to the effects of water vapor clouds that contain black carbon, nitrous oxide, and sulfur dioxide.

Climate scientists use 'radiative forcing' as their measure for how environmentally harmful an activity is. A 2010 study by the University of Oslo’s International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis compared the radiative forcing of car and aircraft travel. The scientists concluded:

"Air travel results in a lower temperature change per passenger-kilometer than car travel on the long run; the integrated radiative forcing of air travel is on short- to medium time horizons much higher than for car travel. Per passenger-hour traveled however, aviation’s climate impact is a factor 6 to 47 higher than the impact from car travel."

One reason the 747 burns so much fuel and has a poor mpg, causing greater environmental harm, is that it's an outdated airframe. This aircraft was first introduced in 1970, and the technology available 56 years ago was substantially less advanced than aircraft technology today.

As a result, the 747 would be considered incredibly inefficient if it were produced today. Furthermore, modern airliners are far lighter than the 747, needing less fuel for takeoff. 21st-century widebody, and notably two-engine, aircraft are far more efficient due to modern technology.

They burn less fuel. However, because they carry fewer passengers than the behemoth 747, they don't necessarily have a better mpg per passenger. The Airbus A350 was introduced in 2015 with Qatar Airways, becoming the first Airbus aircraft constructed primarily with carbon-fibre-reinforced polymers.

Simple Flying reported that this aircraft burns 2,700 gallons per hour, or 0.75 gallons per second. With a cruising speed of 561 mph, the aircraft travels a mile every 6.4 seconds and has a cruising mpg of 0.208. Qantas's upcoming A350-1000s will have 238 seats across four classes, yielding an mpg per passenger of 50. This is equivalent to a modern car with only the driver on board.

A Boeing 787 Dreamliner has also advanced the field of environmentally conscious aviation. The Dreamliner was first introduced in October 2011 with All Nippon Airways. This jetliner burns 2,900 gallons of fuel per hour, and its cruising speed is 561 mph. As a result, the aircraft burns 5.17 gallons per mile, yielding an mpg of 0.193. Meanwhile, a Qantas 787-9 Dreamliner has 236 seats across three classes, so each passenger gets 44.8 mpg during the cruise.

We can see that even modern airliners consume vast quantities of fuel, causing significant environmental harm. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could be a pathway to mitigate the harm of this enormous fuel consumption. SAF is defined as aviation fuel that is not derived from fossil fuels, but has near-identical performance characteristics.

It can be mixed with conventional fuel, and aircraft don't have to be re-engineered. Its development has come with a host of benefits and challenges. IATA's criteria for fuel to be considered sustainable are that it must reduce CO2 emissions across its lifecycle, not require excess freshwater, not compete with food production, and not cause deforestation.

If SAF can be rolled out, it could transform the aviation sector's sustainability. A ScienceDirect study based on the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation found that SAF could allow greenhouse gas emissions to decrease by up to 94%. Airbus puts this number closer to 80%.

SAF has begun to be seen in action within the commercial aviation sector. Virgin Atlantic operated the first 100% SAF flight in 2023, flying a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines. Rolls-Royce has since claimed to be the only engine manufacturer to confirm that all its powerplants work with SAF.

However, SAF rollout has not yet been substantial, primarily due to economic challenges: SAF costs an average of $6 per gallon, while fossil-fuel-based jet fuel typically costs $2.29 per gallon (although it has been on the rise amid the Iran War). The high cost is primarily due to low production rates, as just 33 million gallons of SAF were produced in the US in 2021. The US Department of Energy estimated in 2022 that SAF production would have to increase to 3 billion gallons annually.

#6002. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

Not surprised that someone is jumping on the New Orleans to Honduras market, after the demise of both Spirit and Direct Air, and with TACA/Avianca still not resuming. A surprisingly sizable market, and considering the fares people pay for it, it'd be shocking if anyone left it alone for too long. I wouldn't be surprised to see Southwest jump on it, soon as they figure out how to do efficient currency exchange.

The British Overseas Territory designation was only introduced in 2002; Jamaica and Belize are former British territories (used loosely) that happen to be overseas, but they were never British Overseas Territories.

I don’t understand the controversy. Southwest’s airlines flys to lots of places that are not in the southwest. So they are flying to lots of places not in Bermuda. Why is this an issue? Your post doesn’t explain what the issue is.

I've had a few meetings with their team over the past couple of months. Their strategy is two fold - add service to under served markets (they do not want to compete with AA/DL/UA), and to become the central player for the Caribbean and Central America given the lack of reliable (nas nicer) operators in those regions. While these additions do feel random, they meet those goals. Their new A220s will be a great addition as well. They are also operating a charter business with their planes, which is a pretty unique opportunity and it's more successful than you might think.

Every route originates in a British Overseas territory and the U.S. is an intermediate stop. So for example, Nashville is a one-stop between Grand Cayman and Ocho Rios via Nashville.

#6001. LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

However, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

I remember this happening previously, but I never had an issue with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

First of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

She explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

Irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my issue should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

What’s the most frustrating post-sale customer service experience you’ve had?

@Daniel--I am a bit confused as to why you couldn't enter your alphanumeric post code in the first place. When I book on international websites and they ask for address information, there is usually a field for country. If it didn't, I would say that is LATAM's fault. If the 24 hour refund rule applies, I would say you are entitled to a refund. Of course, I don't work for LATAM. 😃

Hey Daniel! Not sure how long you’ve been living in Brazil, but a very efficieny way to solve these kinds of issues is through a government platform called consumidor.gov. Companies are obligated to answer all complaints filed there in a couple a days or else they pay a hefty fine, and this seems the sort of situtation thats typically addresses through this channel. You have to have a Brazilian CPF number, though, I think, not sure if you have one yet. Hope it helps =)

Hey Daniel! Canadian postal codes also have numbers and letters like in the UK (for example: K1A3R8). This tip works for Canadian credit cards and you can try to see if it works with UK credit cards as well. Whenever you have to type your postal code and the machine (such as self service gas pumps) or website only accepts numbers, type the numbers in your postal code followed by two zeros. So, K1A3R8 becomes 13800. It always works for Canadian credit cards. Try the same with your UK card and it may work. I’m Canadian and Brazilian and this has helped me lots of times to use my Canadian credit card on Brazilian and US websites.

The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia.

Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's new World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built.

Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships.

"Our ambition is simple: To give every guest the best holiday ever," MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago said Wednesday during a dockside ceremony at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard to mark the vessel's official handover to MSC Cruises.

MSC Group is the parent company of MSC Cruises and sister brand Explora Journeys, a luxury line.

"We invested in rethinking spaces, developing new concepts and reshaping the experience," Vago added during remarks from a stage set up just in front of the MSC World Asia's bow.

Vago noted that 60% of the spaces on MSC World Asia are either new or significantly redesigned as compared to the two World Class ships already sailing, MSC World Europa and MSC World America.

Like those two vessels, MSC World Asia has nearly 2,600 rooms and is capable of holding a whopping 6,758 passengers with every berth filled — more than almost any other passenger vessel afloat.

It also has similarly massive dimensions with a length of 1,093 feet — the equivalent of nearly four football fields stacked end-to-end — and a width of 154 feet.

But many of its interior and exterior venues, including a sprawling decktop water park with multiple waterslides and a record-setting dry slide that drops 11 decks, are different from what you'll find on the earlier World Class ships in ways big and small.

Related: The terrifying, record-breaking slide on MSC World Asia

Among the most significant changes is the addition of new dining and food concepts, including MSC Cruises' first pan-Asian restaurant and a Venchi chocolate and gelato venue.

Like the earlier World Class vessels, the ship also offers a sushi bar, teppanyaki restaurant, American-style steakhouse and a branch of the Italian chain Eataly (currently found only on MSC World America), among 20 dining options in all.

In addition to the water park and dry slide, MSC World Asia's top decks offer multiple pool areas; a suspended-over-the-ocean swing ride called The Cliffhangar; and a ropes course.

Notable interior features include a three-deck-high dining and entertainment zone called the World Galleria, which is covered by one of the largest LED-lit ceilings at sea. An outdoor extension of this area, called the World Promenade, features more dining and entertainment, plus a new suspended, illuminated Dragon sculpture — part of the ship's Asia theming.

Related: MSC Cruises cabins and suites guide

The arrival of MSC World Asia marks the latest milestone in MSC Cruises' rapid expansion.

With the addition of MSC World Asia, the brand now operates 24 ships, up from just 13 vessels as recently as 2017. It has nine more on order.

The ships on the way include five more World Class vessels scheduled for delivery by 2031. Also coming is a new class of four somewhat smaller, 180,000-ton vessels that will be known as the Frontier Class.

Wednesday's delivery ceremony included a ceremonial lowering of the Chantiers de l'Atlantique and French flags in front of attendees and the raising of the MSC Cruises flag as well as the flag of Malta, where the vessel is registered.

MSC Group chief financial officer Alexa Aponte Vago, who is married to MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago, served as the traditional "godmother" for the event, which included the smashing of a bottle of Champagne against the ship's hull.

Joining her husband on stage, Alexa Aponte Vago cut a ceremonial blue ribbon to release the bottle of Champagne against the side of the vessel right on the letter C in its name.

While it included a bottle smash, Wednesday's event was not the vessel's official naming. That will take place Saturday in Le Havre, France, at a much larger event.

MSC World Asia will then head to the Mediterranean, where it will begin its first cruises with paying passengers on Dec. 4 with a voyage out of Barcelona.

The ship initially will operate seven-night Mediterranean voyages that include stops in France, Italy, Malta and Spain.

In November 2027, it will reposition to the Southern Caribbean for seven- to 14-night sailings. The itineraries will include stops in Saint Lucia, Grenada, St. Maarten, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

Founded in 1861, the Chantiers d'Atlantique shipyard in St. Nazaire is one of the world's most famous shipyards, known for building many of the world's largest cruise ships as well as naval vessels and wind-powered commercial ships. Notable vessels built at the shipyard include the SS Normandie, SS France, Cunard's Queen Mary 2 and several of Royal Caribbean's Oasis Class ships.

The shipyard has built 20 vessels for MSC Cruises over the past 25 years.

It is located at the mouth of the Loire River on the West coast of France.

#5999. 34-Year-Old FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 Overshoots Runway In Miami, Triggers Ground Stop

*Last Updated: 11:40 PM EST November 25, 2026, by Channing Reid

A McDonnell Douglas MD-11, operated by FedEx Express, overran a runway upon arrival at Miami International Airport (MIA) on Wednesday. The incident triggered the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to impose a ground stop, putting a wrench in the peak of the Thanksgiving travel rush.

It is unclear what may have caused the trijet to veer off the runway, but weather radar indicated rain at the time of landing. It comes less than three months after an Amazon Prime Air-branded Boeing 767-300F overran a runway at MIA, killing five people.

MIA has become fully operational, with all flights allowed to resume. However, delays are estimated to be nearly four hours. Over 530 flights were reported to be delayed as of 11:40 PM.

Miami is the third-most popular tourist destination for Thanksgiving, according to Washington Examiner journalist Anna Giaritelli​​​​​​.

Miami and surrounding areas were dealing with harsh rain conditions around the time of FX910's arrival. The weather in southeast Florida was described as a "black hole," according to Washington Examiner journalist Anna Giaritelli, who reportedly received a text from an off-duty air traffic controller minutes before the MD-11 landed at MIA.

"All the southeast traffic landing miami, lauderdale etc has basically ran into a black hole of weather. Commpand center didn't help us with routes, we lost our land lines to communicate with other facilities, over 10 sever(e) turbulence reports," they explained. "This was absolutely the most dangerous operation I've seen."

Video of the incident obtained by speedbirdHD shows the aircraft passing by on the runway. It appears the crew deployed the aircraft's reverse thrusters, attempting to slow down before overrunning the runway

FedEx confirmed the incident in a statement to Simple Flying on Wednesday. The company said it will coordinate with authorities as the investigation begins.

“FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport. We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA.”

The ground stop was planned to last until 9:45 PM, according to CBS News. Around 9:40 PM, the FAA said the airport would "shortly" become operational again.

"Flights will be resuming shortly at Miami International Airport after FedEx Flight 910 ran off the runway after landing," the agency said. "The McDonnell Douglas MD-11 departed from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis. There are no reports of injuries. The FAA will investigate the incident."

At around 10:45 PM, MIA was gradually accepting some arriving flights via Runway 27 and Runway 30. However, several dozen flights were seen stuck on the tarmac awaiting departure clearances.

MIA officials confirmed that Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident, and there were "no reported injuries." The extent of the damage to the aircraft is unclear. However, the airframe's fuselage did not separate, according to Enilria, indicating that severe external damage may not have been sustained.

Simple Flying contacted FedEx late Wednesday, but representatives could not be immediately reached for comment.

The FAA issued a ground stop at MIA as a result of the runway excursion. The order, however, did not close all runways at the airport. In a statement on social media, MIA officials said all runways were "closed except for runway 9R." The airport also encouraged passengers to check with their airlines for any impacts to flights departing Wednesday night.

"Passengers scheduled to travel tonight are encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport," it said. "We appreciate our passengers’ patience as we work to safely resume normal operations."

According to initial reports from aviation blogger Enilria, the MD-11 overshot the runway at around 8:15 PM after landing amid rain showers at MIA. Flight tracking data indicates the flight, FX910, was operated by N605FE, from FedEx’s hub at Frederick W. Smith International Airport (MEM). The airframe is 34 years old, according to ch-aviation.

The flight pushed back at 4:55 PM local time and took off from MEM at approximately 5:17. Just 20 minutes after departure, the aircraft reached its cruising altitude of 37,000 feet. It maintained the altitude for about an hour and 10 minutes, traveling south, before beginning its descent. At around 6:55 PM EST, data shows the aircraft making a sharp turn southeast as it continued descending through 33,000 feet. It then flew directly toward MIA for about 15 minutes before turning directly east to pass north of the airport.

The plane continued east, passing the coastline, and descended further. It turned back around west to line up for final approach at around 8:17 PM. The aircraft touched down on Runway 26R nine minutes later at 8:26 PM, but failed to stop before overshooting the runway, according to reports.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Yet another incident at KMIA. Thankfully there were no injuries this time. That must be 3 incidents in 3 months. Fingers crossed for no more!
