#5933. Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”

President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

Trump also wrote that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

Various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also announced on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the company’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

We also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the company is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

And we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

Huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his company to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of the investigations’ conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

On “Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions”

#5930. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

#5928. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Your Questions Answered

Questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12

The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on new Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

Premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen said “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

The front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

Skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

With jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

Premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921

Premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium plan 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

Two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135

Two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card company that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

The clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody shows the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

American is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

The premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12

The evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

Unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

Premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

No contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758

American announced the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air New Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

The real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

The industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12

Chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

The local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

New York is where the gap between the big three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting shows three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

American’s disclosed JFK plans are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside new Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

United has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

American’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its New York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

Delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the new Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO said this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

Skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK plan as route and product-level on the current record.

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

Apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The company posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer said the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

The structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

Treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

Points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21

The pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

The open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

For airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23

The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under new silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

The profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

No cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1

U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12

Where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and said explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

The lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

Nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Big Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he says he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15

This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He said chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

JetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

The parts of JetBlue’s current plan that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

One caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a new entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13

The squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

Breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 showed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

Neeleman said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

The commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

Scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Big Four skip.

Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

Neeleman said majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

The practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman said the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

The second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

Reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman said helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the company’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

Breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has said directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13

Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into big cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and said chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

Breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman plans a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its new routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321

Scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The issue is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

The catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 announced changes since early 2025 1.

The unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper said consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45

Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

— Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Allegiant, now merged with Sun Country, serves 42 markets from Fort Lauderdale but only marginally targets former Spirit routes — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City. It is instead adding unique markets no one else flies, expanding the airport’s destination menu.

JetBlue is Fort Lauderdale’s largest carrier and treats it as the third leg of a stool with New York and Boston, adding Mint transcons, domestic first class, and a possible lounge.

The short answer: Allegiant mostly doesn’t compete with JetBlue at FLL head-to-head. It competes around it.

After Spirit shut down in May 2026, JetBlue, Frontier, Breeze, and Allegiant all added capacity at Fort Lauderdale 1. JetBlue went after Spirit’s routes directly, launching 11 new Fort Lauderdale routes on Spirit’s shutdown weekend plus a status match for Free Spirit members 3. Allegiant took a different line: of its 42 Fort Lauderdale markets, only five — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City — were Spirit cities, and it is chasing unique markets instead 1.

That reflects the two models. Allegiant flies low-frequency leisure routes from smaller cities where it is often the only nonstop, so it avoids the daily-frequency, loyalty-driven markets JetBlue serves. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale is built around Northeast traffic, Caribbean and Latin connections — more than 20 routes to Latin America — and premium: Mint lie-flat on transcons to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, with management calling the city “Florida’s biggest premium market” 1. JetBlue is also adding its BlueFirst domestic first class and weighing a Fort Lauderdale lounge 4.

Fort Lauderdale seats excluding Spirit were scheduled up a combined 40% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2026. If demand doesn’t absorb that, the thin unique routes Allegiant favors are the easiest to cut — and JetBlue, which is funding startup losses on new routes while chasing a turnaround, has the most capital at risk.

This question was addressed to Sara Nelson, International President, Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO.

Customer experience and labor-as-cost coexist only when the service promise matches the cost model. The carriers now cutting hardest — KLM, Icelandair, Alaska — are protecting margin under a fuel shock, not reinventing service. The real test is where the cuts land: outsourced ground and contact-center work, and regional crews paid about half mainline, is where the customer actually meets the airline. 326

The fuel shock is forcing the trade-off into the open. Jet fuel was up 102% year over year in mid-September, and record revenue has not covered it 4. American grew revenue 19.3% in Q3 and still posted a 1% operating margin because costs grew 19.7%; Delta and United each slipped about two points 6. Carriers that already settled big contracts — United’s five-year flight attendant deal carries a 31% pay increase and $741 million in retroactive pay — are paying for premium service with loyalty and premium-cabin cash, not by squeezing crew 45.

The unresolved question is whether outsourcing the customer-facing layer — catering, ground handling, contact centers — shows up in the service metrics airlines sell against. KLM has disclosed the cost target and the job moves; it has not disclosed a service standard tied to them.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

India’s fleet orders are not the binding constraint — ground and crew capacity are. Mumbai is rationing international slots to rebuild a terminal, new airports rather than bigger ones are being asked to absorb growth, and tighter pilot duty rules exposed how thin airline crew buffers were. The result: capacity now gets added where slots and crews exist, not where demand is. 1167

Mumbai International Airport told 46 airlines it would pull 265 of Terminal 2’s 770 weekly international departure slots from October 25 to house domestic flights displaced by the Terminal 1 rebuild — IndiGo losing 74 weekly departures, Air India 33, Emirates and Etihad 10 each 1. The ministry intervened, Adani agreed to leave winter slots untouched, and traffic balancing was pushed to the summer 2027 schedule 23. IndiGo and Air India Group then agreed to phase international flying to Navi Mumbai through July 2027 4. The relief valve carries its own friction: Navi Mumbai is 45 km away with no direct metro link expected before 2031, and charges INR 1,225 in passenger fees against INR 615 at Mumbai 4. Adani’s airport CEO expects one or two foreign carriers to suspend Mumbai service for a couple of years rather than split operations 5.

IndiGo canceled more than 1,200 flights after new crew rostering rules collided with thin staffing and system congestion, and the DGCA opened a probe 6. The meltdown deepened — the government rolled back night-flying rules, capped fares, and fined the airline, and it cost IndiGo both profit and its CEO 789. The regulator has since shown it will flex duty rules when airspace disruption lengthens sectors, temporarily relaxing pilot duty-time limits in April 2026 10. Regulators also tied summer schedule approvals to aircraft actually on the ground rather than projected deliveries, forcing airlines to cut planned flying 11.

Skift’s reporting has tracked recruitment to beat an air traffic control officer shortage, with 796 ATC positions created alongside the fleet build-out 12, and CAPA has called for airspace redesign to carry 8–10 times current traffic 13. The sharper near-term airspace problem is geopolitical: Pakistani and Iranian closures pushed IndiGo to suspend Copenhagen and cut UK flying 14, and have hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, moving Air India’s Europe and North America flying toward Mumbai with Bengaluru under study as a third hub 15.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The A220 is what makes Breeze’s network possible: small enough to open thin city pairs no one else serves, long-legged enough to fly them transcon, and cheap enough per trip that Breeze can sit on routes with no nonstop competition. The same airplane caps it. At 137 seats, its unit costs can’t match a densely configured A321neo, so Breeze can’t follow demand into big, contested markets without losing the economics that work. 12

Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, according to Skift Research, and CEO David Neeleman estimates the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 2. He said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — “that’s what got Spirit to die” — and pairs the smaller aircraft with premium seating and bundles to make thin routes work 23.

Charleston, Providence, Hartford, Akron-Canton, Albany, Rochester, Memphis — cities where the Big Three lean on aging regional jets and rivals have pulled seats.

The A220’s range lets Breeze link overlooked eastern cities to Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, and Orange County, plus Las Vegas and Phoenix.

Airline Weekly reported Breeze chases yield premiums instead, and avoids competing against densely configured narrowbodies.

The A220 is a bet that U.S. majors keep upgauging and keep leaving mid-size cities to aging regional jets. That thesis has held. The risk arrives when Southwest’s 737 Max 7 — comparable in size and unit cost — finally shows up in volume, or when a thin market Breeze created attracts a larger airplane.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

The core of Porter’s 2021 case still stands: a 132-seat jet with low trip costs lets it hold daily frequency and keep fares up on routes bigger aircraft can’t fill profitably. What fuel has broken is the financing side. Jet fuel roughly doubled in 2026, Canada has lent money to Porter, Transat, and Flair, and the growth-at-pace ambition behind the 80-aircraft order now runs on borrowed room. 156

The original bet, made in July 2021, had three legs: the E195-E2 was picked over the A220 specifically for lower trip costs; its near-3,000-mile range opened nonstops other carriers only served via connections; and 132 seats against Air Canada and WestJet’s 169-174-seat 737-8s meant Porter could fly thinner markets 2. A fourth leg came with the 2022 product reveal — all-economy with PorterReserve, a premium-economy-light product, rather than following rivals downmarket 3.

Fuel has not invalidated the aircraft choice — it has validated it. Smaller gauge is the right shape for a cost shock, because the fare you need per seat falls with the seats you have to sell. What fuel broke is the balance sheet assumption underneath the order: that Porter could scale a national network on its own money.

Trip-cost economics and frequency — the revenue-side argument for small gauge is stronger at $4-plus fuel, not weaker 1

Self-funded expansion; Porter is now among the Canadian carriers taking government loans 5

Breeze, which protects economics with low trip costs and routes with limited nonstop competition 4

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

Low-cost carriers are genuinely loosening single-fleet discipline — AirAsia on regional jets, Avelo on the E2, IndiGo on widebodies. But slot scarcity isn’t the driver. The reporting points to revenue, not runway access: matching aircraft size to what a market will actually pay, and chasing premium and long-haul revenue the A320/737 can’t reach. Slot-constrained airlines do the opposite — they upgauge within one fleet. 123

The behavior behind the trend is real and spread across more than one region and one type of player. AirAsia’s Tony Fernandes is negotiating with Airbus and Embraer for regional jets, explicitly breaking from the single-type model to serve smaller destinations at higher frequency 2. Avelo ordered up to 100 Embraer E195-E2s alongside its all-Boeing 737 fleet, becoming the first U.S. carrier to commit to the type 3. IndiGo has 60 A350-900s on order, with the first now slipping to the second quarter of 2028 4. Flyadeal has weighed widebodies for high-volume pilgrim and worker routes 7.

What those cases share is a revenue argument, not a capacity-access one. At Skift Aviation Forum, Embraer’s Arjan Meijer pointed to a widening gap between 76-seat regional jets and narrowbodies, and argued that lower per-seat costs can be wiped out by the revenue consequences of flying more seats than a market will absorb at a decent fare 1. Porter’s Kevin Jackson said 132-seat E195-E2s let the airline hold daily service through weak periods and protect unit revenue 1.

Slot constraints produce the opposite response: more seats through the same number of movements, inside one fleet type. EasyJet’s growth at slot-limited Gatwick, Linate, and Charles de Gaulle has come from upgauging A319s and A320s to A320neos and A321neos — roughly 171 seats to 211 — not from adding a second aircraft family 89. British Airways is cutting 52 economy seats per A380 to lift premium cabins to 48% of capacity at Heathrow, again raising revenue per slot rather than diversifying types 10. IndiGo’s A321XLRs on Athens and Amsterdam do protect slots, but that’s a secondary benefit of a long-haul product decision 4.

Fleet simplicity still carries real weight. Cathay ruled out regional jets entirely, citing economies of scale and congested airports 6. Jackson said larger aircraft would suit some Porter routes, but a consistent E2 fleet serves the wider network strategy 1. And Willie Walsh has said IndiGo’s short-haul narrowbody core will not be reshaped to feed long-haul widebodies 5.

If fuel stays elevated and fares keep deciding margins, more LCCs follow Avelo and AirAsia into a second, smaller type to defend yield in thin markets rather than dump seats into them.

Mixed fleets raise crew, maintenance, and spares costs. If the carriers adding types can’t show unit-revenue gains that clear that bill, the discipline snaps back — Cathay’s reasoning becomes the consensus again.

IndiGo’s model — a widebody arm run alongside an untouched narrowbody core — becomes the template for LCCs wanting long-haul without contaminating short-haul costs.

The single-fleet religion is loosening because LCCs are chasing revenue the A320 and 737 can’t capture — in thin markets and in premium and long-haul cabins. Slot scarcity pushes airlines toward bigger aircraft within one family, which is the opposite move.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

Skift’s reporting does not show a Porter plan for replacing its Q400s at Billy Bishop. What the reporting does establish is the constraint that decides the answer: the tripartite agreement bars jets at the island airport, and Ottawa declined to reopen it in 2015, killing Porter’s CS100 order and runway-extension plan. Unless that agreement changes, anything Porter flies downtown has to be a turboprop. 12

Billy Bishop sits on an island in Lake Ontario with a runway of roughly 4,000 feet, restricted to turboprops — Porter’s Q400s already take a weight restriction to operate there 32. Porter’s growth since 2021 has gone the other way: up to 80 Embraer E195-E2s flown from Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, with Billy Bishop kept as the separate downtown base 14. At Skift Aviation Forum this month, Porter President Kevin Jackson said a consistent 132-seat E2 fleet supports the airline’s network strategy, with smaller aircraft preserving frequency for business travelers through weaker periods 5.

The simplest path keeps Billy Bishop inside the existing rules: another regional turboprop type for the downtown operation, run alongside the E2 jet fleet. The cost is the fleet complexity Jackson said the airline has deliberately avoided.

Jets downtown require a runway extension and a change to the agreement that governs the airport. Porter tried that in 2013 with a CS100 order and lost in 2015 when Ottawa declined to review it, with local opposition over noise and the waterfront.

Porter’s jet network already runs from Pearson and eastern Canadian cities, and Billy Bishop’s value — a downtown gate and a U.S. preclearance facility — would have to be weighed against operating a second aircraft type for one airport.

Whether the federal government shows any willingness to revisit the tripartite agreement, and whether Billy Bishop’s U.S. preclearance facility — which Porter, as the airport’s only U.S. operator, stands to benefit from — raises the commercial value of staying downtown enough to justify a second fleet type 6.

Porter’s downtown problem is a regulatory one, not a fleet one. Until the jet ban at Billy Bishop moves, Porter’s only options are another turboprop or a smaller presence on the island.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

One U.S. carrier has ordered the E2: Avelo took 50 firm E195-E2s plus 50 purchase rights in September 2025. The reason no one else has is a weight limit written into major-airline pilot contracts. Scope clauses cap the maximum takeoff weight of jets regional partners may fly, and the re-engined E175-E2 is roughly 13,000 pounds over that line — so the aircraft that would sell in volume cannot legally be flown by the airlines that would buy it. 12

The binding constraint is weight, not seats. Pilot union contracts at the big network carriers restrict the maximum takeoff weight of aircraft operated by regional partners; the E175-E2 comes in at about 99,000 pounds, well above what those contracts generally permit 2. Embraer’s Arjan Meijer called that threshold a “paper limitation” set years before anyone designed an E175 around Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans 2.

SkyWest is the clearest casualty. It ordered 100 E175-E2s in 2013 on the expectation that scope would loosen; it never did, the order was not binding, and SkyWest kept buying first-generation E175s instead — including 20 more for American in early 2020 3. As of 2023, Embraer was still planning to build the older E1 alongside the E2 specifically because U.S. pilot contracts kept E1 demand alive 4.

The workaround is to skip the regional model entirely. Avelo is an independent ultra-low-cost carrier with no scope clause to satisfy, so it could order the larger E195-E2 outright, with deliveries from 2027 1. Porter Airlines in Canada has built a network on 132-seat E195-E2s, and its president Kevin Jackson argued at Skift Aviation Forum that the smaller gauge protects frequency and daily service through weak periods rather than chasing the lowest cost per seat 5.

This question was addressed to Robin Hayes, Chairman and CEO of Airbus in North America, Airbus.

Skift’s reporting doesn’t show an active ME3 campaign to relaunch the A380, and the conditions that would make Airbus say yes aren’t there. Emirates’ traffic fell 22% and its seat factor dropped to 72% in the half to September 30, with fuel at 34% of operating cost. A four-engine, 500-seat jet is the worst possible aircraft in a fuel shock. Airbus is sold out on the A350 instead. Likelihood: very low. 14

The demand case the Gulf carriers once made for the A380 rested on slot-constrained airports and reliably full hubs. Both legs are weaker now. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers in the six months to September 30, down 22%, with capacity down 17% and seat factor at 72% from 79.5%, as the U.S.-Iran war pushed connecting traffic toward Istanbul and Singapore 1. Its first-half profit fell 66% to $899 million and survived only on $1.93 billion of hedging gains; analyst Linus Benjamin Bauer said the core flying business was likely loss-making unhedged 1. Emirates’ growth had already plateaued before the war on Dubai airport congestion, with FlyDubai taking the expansion role 5.

What the Gulf carriers are actually buying is the answer. Emirates ordered 65 more Boeing 777Xs for $38 billion at the 2025 Dubai Airshow 2, holds more than 340 aircraft on order worth about $150 billion, and is spending more than $7 billion retrofitting existing jets rather than seeking new very-large aircraft 1. Etihad went the other way entirely, ordering 30 A321LRs and putting first class on a narrowbody 6. Qatar Airways’ Hamad Al-Khater said the airline is working with Boeing on the delayed 777X and has 138 aircraft arriving over five years 9.

Airbus has the opposite problem to an empty line. Widebody demand is running hard into supply chain, labor, and production constraints, with the A350 backlog already deep 4. Restarting a closed four-engine program would compete for the same engineers, suppliers, and slots that Airbus is using to deliver aircraft it has already sold.

Emirates has refitted aircraft inside a program valued at more than $7 billion, and British Airways is cutting its A380s from 469 to 417 seats to lift premium share to 48%. Existing airframes absorb premium demand without a new program.

Fleet strategy debate has centered on a possible stretched A350 rather than a new superjumbo — a derivative Airbus can build on a line that is already running.

Emirates added 65 777Xs for $38 billion and Qatar Airways says it is working closely with Boeing on the delayed program. The large-twin answer is already ordered, just late.

The A380 keeps its fans in the Gulf and at Heathrow, but the money is going into retrofits, twins, and narrowbodies. Airbus closed the line because the orders weren’t there, and a demand picture weaker than 2019’s doesn’t reopen it.

This question was addressed to Darren Hulst, VP, Commercial Marketing, Boeing.

Boeing’s delivery performance to Ryanair improved because Boeing slowed itself down first, then rebuilt the system around quality and regulatory sign-off. Ryanair’s complaints have shifted from defective, late aircraft to a more basic constraint: there aren’t enough slots.

How Boeing’s Ryanair Deliveries Turned Around

O’Leary said only 40 of 57 expected 737 Max deliveries would arrive on time, forcing frequency cuts at high-cost airports.

O’Leary said Max jets were arriving with fewer defects, citing better fuselages shipped from Wichita to Seattle, and asked Boeing for a plan to accelerate deliveries.

The FAA acknowledged improvements in Boeing’s safety management, opening the door to higher 737 Max production, though delays still forced changes at Southwest and Ryanair.

Airline Weekly cited improving Max deliveries and a widening unit-cost advantage as Ryanair headed into a strong peak summer.

Boeing’s 737 chief Katie Ringgold said traveled work was down about 60% in a year, suppliers were all at rate 42, and the next step to 47 a month would come in late spring or early summer 2026.

Ryanair’s last 29 Gamechanger Max deliveries were each defect-free and arrived one to two months ahead of their revised dates, O’Leary said, praising Kelly Ortberg and Stephanie Pope.

Quality control at the fuselage source. Spirit AeroSystems, which builds 737 Max fuselages in Wichita, was brought back inside Boeing. O’Leary flagged better fuselage quality as early as 2024, before the acquisition closed 32.

Deliberate slowdown. Boeing cut output in 2024 to install stricter inspections and “move-ready” criteria. Ringgold said Boeing built fewer aircraft than customers needed as a result, and that those processes now show up as better quality and flow 2.

The FAA became a gatekeeper. After the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout, the FAA capped 737 output at 38 a month and now formally approves every rate increase. Boeing was cleared to 42 in November 2025 2.

The improvement Ryanair is praising is partly an artifact of lowered expectations: those 29 aircraft arrived early against delivery dates that had already slipped by roughly a year. The durable gain is defect-free handover, which cuts Ryanair’s own acceptance and rework time.

All of Ryanair’s Max 8s have been delivered. Its 300-aircraft Max 10 order is now the live question, with first delivery scheduled for spring 2027 and running through 2034 1. Boeing certified the Max 7 in August 2026 after about a decade of delays and was targeting Max 10 certification by year-end 7.

Delivery reliability also matters more than usual right now. Ryanair cut its FY27 traffic target to 214 million passengers and reported a 15% drop in half-year profit after tax to €2.1 billion, with a €2 billion fuel bill increase coming in fiscal 2027/28 8. Newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft are one of the few cost levers that don’t require a fight with a union or an airport.

This question was addressed to Juha Jaervinen, Chief Customer Officer, Virgin Atlantic.

British Airways’ A380 refit — 52 seats out, premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft — concentrates high-yield passengers behind a single slot at a Heathrow where BA can’t simply add a flight 1. Virgin Atlantic is running the same play at Heathrow, and started earlier: economy on refurbished 787s drops from 192 seats to 127, and new A330s carry 104 premium seats against 128 in economy 34.

Doyle called it one of BA’s most significant aircraft transformations. IAG’s Gallego said the heavier premium configuration would not work across every IAG market.

Koster said Virgin had been underweight in premium since the A340-600 and called the shift an investment rather than a bet.

Virgin has already chosen speed of conversion over amenity: the onboard bars, among its most recognizable brand assets, are being replaced with more spacious private seats 2. That is the cleanest counter to BA adding suites — Virgin converts the square footage it was spending on social space into sellable Upper Class.

The second lever is the ground product, where Virgin is investing in the JFK Clubhouse and expanded Retreat Suites against BA’s new Heathrow Terminal 5C lounge, due at the end of 2028 21. The third is the Delta joint venture, which Koster said gives Virgin network and scale while leaving the challenger brand intact 3.

Virgin Atlantic isn’t being forced to respond to BA’s A380 refit — it moved first, and more aggressively relative to its fleet. The open question is yields: BA, Virgin, American, Alaska, Emirates, and Turkish are all adding premium seats into the same cycle, and Skift reporting flags crowding as the risk if supply grows faster than the pool of payers.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

Airlines control the single biggest lever for tier-2 and tier-3 growth — where they put seats. Crisil’s data shows capacity deployment, not demand, is what turned Hindon and Kannur into million-passenger airports. But that lever only works where an airport, a usable aircraft type, and viability support already exist, and all three are government-set. Airlines can move the needle hard on existing regional airports; they can’t create the next 100. 12

Regional airports make up 58% of India’s airports but carry just 2-3% of domestic traffic, and that share has gone backwards — from 3.4% in the 2021 and 2022 financial years to 2.3% in fiscal 2025 1. Crisil’s read is that the UDAN scheme’s importance has been “more structural than volumetric” 1. Where airlines did add capacity, the numbers moved fast: Hindon and Kannur each crossed 1 million annual passengers in fiscal 2025 on the back of increased deployment, and Agra, Hindon, and Tezpur grew traffic 7-10x between fiscal 2020 and 2025 against 120% national growth 1.

Two things cap what airlines can do on their own. First, fleet: only about 80 dedicated regional transport aircraft fly in India, and the government projects a need for roughly 100 a year over the next decade 2. Narrowbodies don’t make 45-to-90-minute thin routes work. Second, economics: only about 5% of Indian domestic seat capacity sits on regional routes, compared with roughly double that in the U.S. and Europe, and 68% of domestic traffic touches one of the 10 busiest airports 8.

The current cycle also works against small-city flying. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter, with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, and recovered only about 60% of the fuel increase through fares 5. Capacity under that pressure goes to dense trunk routes and international flying, not 70-seat regional hops. Akasa has named tier-2 and tier-3 cities as central to its domestic strategy 6, and Fly91 was built specifically for the gap 7, but neither carries the scale to change the national mix alone.

Airlines decide whether India’s existing regional airports fill up — that is a real, provable lever worth multiples of traffic at individual airports. They do not decide whether the next tier of cities gets an airport, a subsidy, or an aircraft small enough to serve it profitably, and that is where the 2-3% national share is actually set.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The single highest-impact move is closing the fuel-recapture gap — pricing and capacity discipline that turns a $4.64-a-gallon cost into fare revenue. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, so the premium bet can’t rescue 2027. JetBlue recaptured only 50% of fuel costs in Q2 2026, and it guided to a negative 4.5% to negative 6.5% operating margin. Fuel is where the margin went. 142

Everything else JetBlue is doing — premium cabins, Fort Lauderdale growth, lower-cost terminals, loyalty — matters, but on a slower clock. BlueFirst should add nearly five points of revenue per available seat mile, according to president Marty St. George, yet the retrofit doesn’t finish until late 2028 because of supply chain bottlenecks 31. The $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 a gallon; JetBlue paid $4.23 in Q2 2026 and expects $4.64 in Q4 42.

JetBlue has the right long-term plan and the wrong timetable. The premium and loyalty build-out pays off in 2028; the fuel bill is due now, which makes pricing power and capacity cuts the only levers that move 2027.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neither lever works alone. Fares recapture the cost only with a lag — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, below its own 80%-90% guidance. The carriers holding margin are pairing price with capacity discipline and revenue that doesn’t ride on a seat: premium mix, loyalty, cargo, and at Delta, a refinery. Operations decide who survives the lag. 15

Revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% year over year in the third quarter while operating profit was roughly flat 2. That gap is the whole argument: pricing is working, and it still isn’t enough on its own. Average domestic airfare is up about 32% year over year, per Kayak, and demand has held 3.

The limits of the fare lever are clearest at Ryanair. Michael O’Leary said covering a €2 billion ($2.24bn) fuel increase through fares alone would need average ticket prices up about 20%, or €10 per passenger — and he doesn’t expect that, so Ryanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, and cheaper airport deals 4.

The deciding variable is the lag, not the lever. United’s CFO attributed the shortfall to the speed of the late-quarter spike rather than weak demand, and said United is highly confident it can recapture 100% — with a lag. Carriers with short booking curves reprice fast: Air Canada’s transborder unit revenue rose 24% year over year on close-in bookings while its longhaul passengers flew on fares booked before the spike. Operations buy the time that pricing needs.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Expect fares to rise again over the next year, though more slowly than the step-change of 2026. The driver is cost, not demand. Jet fuel hit record levels this year — September’s $4.37 a gallon U.S. average was an all-time high — and carriers have been passing it through 6. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs through pricing in Q3 and says it will close the gap to 100% next year, with a lag 6.

Three forces point up. Scott Kirby is planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and argues fares are still below 2019 in real terms 6; he has said airlines can pass the cost on, helped by Spirit’s collapse removing cheap domestic seats 8. American’s Robert Isom said there is more room to raise fares, and is slowing 2027 growth to protect profitability 6. Ancillaries are moving the same way — JetBlue raised bag fees twice in 2026 4.

Two forces cap the increase. Capacity growth is picking up just as airlines push price, with weak consumer sentiment in the background, Melius Research’s Conor Cunningham warned 8. And the low-cost end can’t follow: Ryanair’s O’Leary said covering his fuel bill would need fares about 20% higher, said he doesn’t expect that, and is cutting costs instead 3.

Europe is on a different clock. Hedges cushioned this year — Ryanair fares actually fell 2% in Q3 — but shorthaul fares inflected upward in August and are now modestly ahead of last year as carriers cut capacity, and the cheap hedges expire in 2027 12.

This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

Structurally higher fuel for three years doesn’t break demand — it breaks the weakest cost structures. Expect fares and fees to stay up, capacity growth to be rationed to routes that clear a higher hurdle, premium and loyalty to carry more of the P&L, and a thinning of unhedged, low-fare operators. United’s Scott Kirby is already planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and predicts weaker U.S. carriers will have to cut flying. 12

The pass-through is real but slow. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in the third quarter, up from about 50% in the second and short of the 80%–90% it guided to over the summer, leaving roughly $500 million unrecovered in one quarter 1. Delta attributed its entire 2026 guidance cut — to $5.10–$``{=html}5.60 per share from $6.50–$``{=html}7.50 — to fuel, and about $6 billion in added expense this year 3. Over three years, that lag compounds into permanently repriced tickets: domestic airfares are already up about 30% this year 4.

Three years of expensive fuel is a sorting mechanism, not a demand shock. Carriers with premium cabins, loyalty cash, and hedges reprice and keep flying; unhedged short-haul and low-fare operators cut, shrink fleets, or exit. IAG’s Luis Gallego said strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill — that option isn’t available to everyone.

This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

No single lever covers a fuel bill that doubled in 2026. Fares do most of the work — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, up from about 50% in Q2 — with capacity cuts, bag fees, premium and loyalty revenue, hedging, cargo, and labor cost closing the rest. Carriers with hedges, premium demand, or cargo are coping; those without are cutting flying. 91

Fuel averaged $4.41 a gallon in early November, and was 111% higher year over year in the week ending Oct. 9 311. Revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% in Q3 while operating profit was roughly flat 1.

Raise faresDomestic airfare is up about 30-32% this year. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3 and expects a similar rate in Q4, having pushed back its 100% target; Q3 fuel rose $1.8 billion, leaving about $500 million unrecovered in one quarter. 3912

Cut capacityAmerican will slow 2027 growth, with Q4 capacity up 5.5-6.5% against roughly 2% at Delta and United. United says it will cut marginal routes; Ryanair cut its winter traffic target by two million passengers and European carriers trimmed capacity, which turned Q4 fares modestly positive. 10112

Ancillary feesJetBlue raised checked bag fees twice in 2026, to $50 from $45 for a first bag booked more than 24 hours out, and a spokesperson said the increase offsets rising fuel and operating costs while keeping base fares competitive. 3

Premium and loyalty mixPremium cabins produced 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion. United’s premium and loyalty revenue each rose 17% in Q3 and contracted business revenue rose 26%. IAG’s Luis Gallego said strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill. 791

HedgingEurope’s big groups absorbed the spike better because they are hedged — Ryanair at about 80% for the year to March 2027 at roughly $67abarrel.EmiratesstayedprofitableonlyonAED7.1billion($``{=html}1.93 billion) in hedging gains, which cut a 60% pre-hedge fuel increase to 13% net. Hedges expire: Ryanair is only 25% hedged at $95forthefollowingyearandfacesa€2billion($``{=html}2.24bn) fuel increase. 2134

Cut other costs, and sell cargoRyanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, cheaper airport deals, and more AI in back-office work, after O’Leary said covering the gap on fares alone would need about 20% higher prices. Air Canada recaptured close to 100% of incremental fuel costs through cargo; Emirates’ SkyCargo revenue rose 52% on volumes down 1%. Alaska is cutting 200 back-office jobs. 4513

The lever that decides outcomes is the booking curve, not the tactic. Air Canada’s transborder routes, which book close in, posted a 24% unit revenue surge, while longhaul passengers who booked 60 to 120 days out are flying on pre-spike fares. Recovery lags the price move, so the open question is how much further fares can rise before demand responds — IATA September traffic was down nearly 1% year over year. 5

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

Air India figures submitted to Indian officials; the airline has separately put the cost at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year.

Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, and the ban has been extended repeatedly 1. Nearly two years on, the economics are visible in three places: fuel burn, network design, and competitive position.

Fuel and block time. Air India told Indian officials the closure pushed fuel costs up by as much as 29% and added up to three hours on some long-haul flights, costing roughly $455 million a year in profit before tax 1. In a separate accounting it put the figure at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year 2.

Routes that no longer pay. Air India suspended Delhi–Washington in August 2025 and has struggled to run Mumbai– and Bengaluru–San Francisco efficiently 1. It cut or suspended services to North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia between June and August 2026, citing airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices 5. IndiGo suspended Copenhagen and trimmed UK flying 6.
